In a way, yes, because I would not like to introduce to-night controversial matters. But it has a very interesting bearing on German as well as on British imperialism. Parliament agreed upon the necessity of doing something. The Liberal government came out with a policy that was defined by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, of building up a Canadian navy, Canadian in time of peace and imperial in time of war. It was rather a queer policy. Later on, the Conservative party in the House of Commons came with a counter proposal of a contribution to the British navy.
Perhaps it may not be out of place, not for the sake of resurrecting old arguments, but simply to show on what principle or basis of argument we rely to oppose these changes in our relations with the United Kingdom without any thoughtful reflection being given to it, if I now read a resolution which was adopted after the election in Drummond-Arthabaska, and framed if I may mention it by myself in conjunction with the late Mr. Monk, later on Minister of Public Works in the Borden government. It reads thus:
This meeting approves and ratifies the verdiet rendered by t-he electoral division of Drummond and Arthabaska; re-affirms the will of the Canadian people to uphold the rights of the British crown in Canada; declares itself ready to approve of all necessary and efficient measures to make sure the defence of Canadian territory. But it considers as contrary to the principle of Canadian autonomy and the real unity of the empire, any policy tending to impose upon Canada, that has no voice in the government of the Empire, any share in the external responsibilities or in the military defence of the Empire, outside of the Canadian territory-the only portion of the Empire upon -which the Canadian people may exercise any political or constitutional action.
This after all was a mere enunciation in a condensed form of all the principles and policies that had been laid down for half a century; that had been supported by argument and by correspondence; that had been applied in practice as well as upheld in doctrine by the leaders of the two great parties whether in opposition or in power. It seems to me therefore that there was no reason for one party to attack the other on this ground in the province

Canada's Imperial Relations
of Quebec, while denouncing and combating the men who were instrumental in maintaining that policy.
At the following session, after Mr. Monk had moved an amendment to the Address in conformity with this resolution, Mr. Borden, leader of the Conservative party, moved a subamendment; but when his sub-amendment had been defeated he rallied himself with all his party in support of Mr. Monk's motion which was nothing but a confirmation of the policy asserted in Drummond-Arthabaska. It was then that Mr. Borden very properly laid down this policy in the name of the Conservative party:
I think the question of Canada's co-operation upon a permanent basis in imperial defence involves very large and wide considerations. If Canada and the other dominions of the empire are to take part as nations of this Empire in the defence of the empire as a whole, shall it be that we. contributing to that defence of the whole empire, shall have absolutely, as citizens of this country, no voice whatever in the councils of the empire touching the issues of peace or war throughout the empire? I do not think that such would be a tolerable condition; I do not think the people of Canada would for one moment submit to such a condition. Shall members of this House, representative men, representing 221 constituencies of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, shall no one of them have the same voice with regard to those vast imperial issues that the humblest taxpayer in the British Isles has at this moment? It does not seem to me that such a condition would make for the integrity of the empire, for the closer co-operation of the empire. Regard must be had to these far-reaching considerations.
If it were legitimate, proper, for the leader of the Conservative party in 1910 to lay down and to express in such clear terms the doctrine of Dominion autonomy, of equality of right with the United Kingdom in matters of foreign policy, why should we be branded as traitors to the crown because we persist in saying that this is the true and the only principle upon which it is possible to maintain the dignity of the various component parts of the empire, and at the same time that unity which has been and will be found under British rule alone as long as British rule means liberty of opinion and liberty of action?
The next year the Imperial conference dealt with these matters. It was probably one of the most interesting of those Imperial conferences. It came before the war, before our minds were troubled by the anxieties of the war, and close enough to the war to enable far-seeing statesmen to see what complications would arise in connection with inter-imperial relations, in case of a war in Europe. At that conference, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, Sir Joseph Ward, a staunch imperialist with a logical mind, came with a motion in favour of the organization
of an Imperial council to deal with all these matters and to enable the various portions of the empire to stand on a footing of equality. To this the Prime Minister of England, Mr. Asquith, made this reply:
For what does Sir Joseph Ward's proposal come to?
I might describe the effect of it, without going into details, in a couple of sentences. It would impair, if not altogether destroy, the authority of the government of the United Kingdom in such grave matters as the conduct of foreign policy, the conclusion of treaties, the declaration and maintenance of peace, or the declaration of war, and, indeed, all those relations with foreign powers, necessarily of the most delicate character, which are now in the hands of the Imperial government, subject to its responsibility to the Imperial parliament.
And he added these significant words:
That authority cannot be shared.
That was a pretty clear and stiff declaration. It passed, but later on, after the change of government had taken place in Canada, Sir Robert Borden, Prime Minister of Canada-whom I will always credit with some of the most timely and courageous declarations that have been made in favour of Canadian autonomy and whose pertinacity of thought in this matter has rendered great services to Canada and the empire-Sir Robert Borden, when proposing his naval contribution, came out with this declaration, very interesting because it combines at once the statement of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman in 1907 and this late declaration of Mr. Asquith in 1911:
Responsibility for the empire's defence upon the high seas, in which is to be found the only effective guarantee of its existence, and which has hitherto been assumed by the United Kingdom, has necessarily carried with it responsibility for and control of foreign policy.
This is practically a repetition of Sir Hemy Campbell-Bannerman's statement in 1907.
When Great Britain no longer assumes sole responsibility for defence upon the high seas-
Naturally, I repeat, this applies to land war operations outside of the country.
-she can no longer undertake the same sole responsibility for and sole control of foreign policy which is closely, vitally, and constantly associated with that defence in which the dominions participate. It has been declared in the past, and even during recent years, that responsibility for foreign policy could not be shared by Great Britain with the dominions. In my humble opinion, adherence to such a position could have but one and that a most disastrous result. During my recent visit to the British Islands, I ventured on many public occasions to propound the principle that the great dominions, sharing in the defence of the empire upon the high seas, must necessarily be entitled to share also in the responsibility for and in the control of foreign policy. No declaration that I made was greeted more heartily and enthusiastically than this. It is satisfactory to know that to-day not only His Majesty's ministers but also the leaders of the opposite political party in Great Britain have explicitly accepted this principle and have affirmed their conviction that

Canada's Imperial Relations
the means by which it can be constitutionally accomplished must be sought, discovered and utilized without delay.
The answer was not slow to come. This was pronounced on the 5th December, 1912; and on the 10th December, Mr. Harcourt, Colonial Secretary, sent a despatch explaining the position. He said:
The Canadian government having changed in the autumn of 1911 it w*as necessary, when Mr. Borden and his colleagues visited England this summer, to put these proposals before them, as they were, of course, unaware of the previous proceedings. Subject to consultation with his colleagues in Canada, Mr. Borden provisionally accepted the resolutions as passed and stated that he saw no difficulty in one of 'his ministers either with or without portfolio spending some months in London in order to carry out this intention. Mr. Asquith and I had, subsequently, several private conversations with him, at which he expressed the desire that the Canadian and other dominions ministers who might be in London as members of the committee of imperial defence should receive, in confidence, knowledge of the policy and proceedings of the Imperial government in foreign and other affairs.
Mind you, a very reasonable request, just to have knowledge of what was going on.
We pointed out -to him that the Committee on Imperial Defence is a purely advisory body and is not and cannot under any circumstances become a body deciding on po?icjr, which is and must remain the sole prerogative of the British cabinet, subject to the support of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom.
Now, I do not dispute the soundness of this policy from a practical point of view. I quite realize the difficulties in which these men in London find themselves, when from day to day they must keep in touch with what is going on in Africa, in Asia, in Europe and elsewhere, keep up their diplomatic correspondence with all their ambassadors and ministers and consuls, keep in touch with all foreign governments, and so forth. I quite realize the difficulty, not to say impossibility, which they must experience in keeping governments in Ottawa, in Melbourne, in Capetown and in other parts of the empire equally informed as to what is transpiring, and the still greater difficulty of getting the sense of these various governments in respect of any policies that are propounded. Very well; I fully appreciate the situation. But, then, is it not a natural consequence that so long as a means is not found of putting the selfgoverning dominions on an equal footing of responsibility with the United Kingdom, it is unfair, it is unjust, it is un-British to ask those outlying dominions to share the same consequences ensuing from imperial policy as the people of England and Scotland and Wales, who at every by-election or general election can reach by their votes the men whom they hold responsible for such policy, and can re-
ward them if they have done well by their country' or punish them if they have betrayed their trust?

It is worse than that. What I have always maintained, and what I have stated to-night, is that for the past twenty-five years a growing number of Canadians have lost their sense of British citizenship to such a degree that they' are prepared to assume burdens which the British people would never think of undertaking themselves, or of imposing upon us.

Of course it does. I
should not like to do so, but if my hon. friend grates upon my British nerves I may be tempted to make a comparison.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
This surprises hon. gentlemen, but they are so much imbued with the modern Yankee type of imperialism that they do not realize how it is possible for a man, foreign by blood to British institutions, to be deeply attached to those institutions. It is not an attachment of blood with me, but purely one of reason; and therefore I am not carried away by impulse in these matters. I try to reason them out. In my reasoning I may be wrong, but I nevertheless claim the right to remain faithful to principles which I believe to be sound, principles that have been respected for a full century as constituting the only safe basis of imperial relations. I claim the right as a Canadian and a British subject to remain faithful to that ideal without being branded a rebel or a dialoyal French-Canadian. The fact is that not being English by language, nor American by mentality, nor Prussian in spirit, I choose to remain British in the sense in which our Canadians were British fifty years ago. And here my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Per-ley) may begin to realize the distinction I draw between an ordinary British-Canadian and what I call an ardent imperialist.

Canada's Imperial Relations
Now 'the Great war came on with none of these problems settled, but all of them raised before the people of the various British communities in a haphazard manner. This is not the time to discuss whether or not Canada or any other of the British dominions ought not to have entered the war. I merely mention one outstanding feature of the whole thing, with which everyone agrees, apart from a few eccentrics, namely, that each dominion was free to participate in the war or to refrain from doing so, as it might see fit. Everyone shared that view. IMr. Bonar Law, among other British statesmen, was of the opinion that neither Canada, nor Australia, nor New Zealand, nor South Africa had any obligation whatever to take part in the war. But if any dominion undertook to go in it, it meant a tremendous contribution in men and money to the new doctrine of imperial solidarity. I say it meant a contribution to the doctrine of imperial solidarity, for it cannot be pleaded that either Canada or Australia went into the war as full-fledged nations. No; had they entered the war in the status of full nationhood they would have been obliged to make a declaration of war against Germany, Austria, Bulgaria and Turkey, according to the time that those countries entered the conflict. Before even England had declared war, the government of Canada had sent a despatch to London offering tiroops. True, parliament was convened after the offer had been made, but in point of fact no declaration of war was ever served in the name of Canada to the German or the Austrian governments. How, therefore, did Canada come to take part in the war? No one has ever answered that question precisely. It is admitted on every hand1 that the declaration of war by the British government could not commit us to -action, although of course it did render the territory of Canada liable to attack from the enemies of Great Britain. Everyone is agreed on that point, But according to the doctrine and practice that had been followed up to the South African war and maintained during that war, a declaration of war by the British government did not carry with it any obligation on the .part of any of the selfgoverning dominions to enlist one man or to spend one dollar. I do not think I need labour that point; it has been acknowledged not only in England but in every one of the self-governing dominions as an incontrovertible principle. Well, then, how did we come to participate in the war? I leave aside to-night, of course, the very eloquent reasons that were advanced during the war-the defence of democracy, the assertion of the principle of self-determination, and all that. Let us suppose that those had been .the true reasons: they would nevertheless have imposed upon us the necessity of declaring war upon the enemies of the empire just as the United States did in 1917. The fact is, we went into the war without any declaration of war on our part because of the new doctrine of imperial solidarity, irrespective of the geographical situation of any of the selfgoverning dominions, and irrespective equally of the local or particular causes of war which any of those dominions might have against Germany at that time or against any other country subsequently. This is what was new.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. member if he thinks we did wrong?

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend frankly. The hon. gentleman must know, or he might ask some of his friends who know me, that I am not afraid of saying anything. I stated at the beginning of the war that I thought we did right, but I added this: First, that parliament should have declared, previous to its decision to participate in the war, that it reserved for the free and peaceful will of the people of Canada to decide what would be her future relations with the empire, and should not have acknowledged the principle of imperial solidarity as opposed to the principle of dominion autonomy that had been sustained heretofore. That was the first reservation. The second was this: I considered that Canada should have measured her participation in that war according to her means of action, according to the number of her population and according to her future needs, not only as regarded herself, but as regarded her true contribution to the British Empire, which will never be so efficacious as when we accomplish it on the soil of Canada by making Canada populous, prosperous and happy. In the light of what has transpired since, I would not now say that we did right in going to war. But I repeat, I do not say it was wrong then. I do not blame those men who voted in sincerity for the participation of Canada in the war; but I say, first, they departed from the established practice and principle upon which the relations between Great Britain and Canada had been carried on for a century, and happily for both countries; and, second, that this having been done, they must be prepared now to stand manfully in a broad way the consequences of that participation. Surely there is not a representative of the people of Canada, whether he be French or English by birth, whether he

Canada's Imperial Relations
be Conservative, Liberal or Progressive by party affiliation, who will come to me and say that after we have spent in four years' time as much money as we had spent in fifty years' time to build up this country', after we have made greater sacrifices for England and France than generations of Canadians had been called to make for Canada, after we have either compromised or endangered the solution of every national, provincial, racial or economic problem of this country in order to come to the rescue of England and France,-surely not one such representative will tell me that this is not the time to study the problem, and that we have only to look upon the past actions of this or that gentleman in some little street in a Canadian city, town or village. No Sir! The most patriotic and practical men of England and Australia, of South Africa and New Zealand, have been concerning themselves with this problem for the last ten years. This coming fall the Prime Minister of Canada, whether he be this right hon. gentleman or the other right hon. gentleman-the purely party of point of view for the present time I want to forget-will go to London, and with men representing the free peoples of Australia and the other outstanding dominions will discuss those problems with the representatives of Great Britain. Is it improper that as a Canadian, tracing my ancestry back through generations of Canadians, I should desire that some one will speak out in those councils of empire with the same thoughtful voice and after the same due reflection that the representatives of the other portions of the British Empire will carry there? Is this improper? Is this unpatriotic? Is this disturbing the House of Commons from the tremendous problem of whether certain gentlemen painted in blue shall take the place of certain other gentlemen tinted in red? I repeat with Lionel Curtis: this issue of peace and war, of relations between Great Britain and the sister dominions, out of which the maintenance or the downfall of the British Empire may be assured in the next twenty-five years, is predominant over all other domestic issues that we may have to deal with; because according to the solution that will be given to this supreme issue, the other issues will be governed and directed and finally settled.
Now, have we progressed in the way of participation in the government of the empire in the same proportion as we have progressed in our contribution to the war expenditure of the empire? Not later than last fall Sir Robert Borden-who is now free to speak his mind, who has no longer the re-

sponsibility of a government or a party, and who, I am happy to say, has preserved his freshness of mind and his constitutional knowledge-went to a very interesting yearly gathering, the Institute of Politics of Williamstown College, Massachusetts. He spoke there on August 17, 1925. He did not think, as did our good friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy), that it was not worth while speaking of this, that we should wait till the fire is burning the house to know what measures we rvill take to extinguish it. No! Sir Robert, ever since he quit politics, has lost no occasion of talking on these matters and, I think, on the whole, very sensibly. He spoke of the part which the dominions played during the war in framing the war policy. He spoke of the imperial war council, and he defined it as:
A consultative body in which all important questions respecting the conduct of -the war snd the war effort of the empire were discussed and determined, and in which dominion -ministers sat on terms of perfect *equality with their British colleagues.
Then he spoke of the imperial war conference of 1917:
The well-known resolution -passed by this conference to which the British government was a party, based the constitutional relations of the empire -upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations of an imperial commonwealth, and Of India as an important -portion of the same, confirmed the right of the dominions and India to an adequate voice in foreign policy a-nd foreign relations, and declared the necessity of -providing effective arrangements for continuous consultation and necessary concerted action.
My old friend Sir Robert still has an affection for the adjective, "adequate." -I remember when he spoke of "adequate protection." Of course, that is pretty difficult to define. Let us see how in practice that adequate voice granted to the dominions and to India in the various conferences or congresses in which they took part during the war and since the war was heard.
First there was a negotiation which resulted in these instruments of diplomacy-I will not say of peace-which followed the war: the treaty of Versailles, the treaty of Trianon, the treaty of St. Germain, and so forth. There was one Dominion statesman who saw through them, or at least who saw through the treaty of Versailles. That man was General Smuts, who, -before affixing 'his signature, entered a solemn -protest -because, as he said, "This will not -bring peace." I think events have proven that he was perhaps the most clearsighted of all the British representatives there. I have been told by one very close to the peace negotiators that forty-eight hours before that so-called instrument of peace, the Versailles treaty, containing the covenant of

Canada's Imperial Relations
the League of Nations, with nearly four hundred articles and appendices, was signed, not one of the Dominion representatives had read it. I do not know. There is one thing I do know, however, that at the next meeting of the League of Nations at Geneva, the Hon. Mr. Doherty, Minister of Justice in the late Conservative government and representative of Canada, wanted article 10 of the covenant of the league to be revised in such a manner as to resurrect in different form the old doctrine of colonial and dominion autonomy, although it was not stated in so many words. Later on Sir Lomer Gouin, Minister of Justice and representative of the Canadian government at the following conference, also endeavoured to have a revision of that article, He came closer to the goal, but did not succeed. There it stands, committing Canada with all the other full-fledged nations, nations able to frame their policy and constitution to their needs and having the right of self-government in foreign as well as international matters. We stand committed by signatures made in haSte by our representatives because they were told to rely upon the wisdom of the British representatives.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say I have not heard of Sir Robert Borden's protest. I do not find it anywhere in the documents relating to the Peace conference.

the reports.

Yes, unofficial reports,
but even then that strengthens my contention that in that so-called association of nations which took its first form in Paris, an article was introduced in the treaty which was supposed to govern in the future the relations of the British Empire at large with all other nations. It was supposed, as a consequence, to govern the inter-imperial relations of the various British dominions whose representatives affixed their signatures. There was an article framed in closed chamber between Mr. Wilson, Mr. Orlando-no, he was not there- Mr. Clemenceau and Mr. Lloyd George, which forced Sir Robert Borden, as representing Canada, to enter a protest which is not noted in the international documents, and which has no official bearing. Later on, when Mr. Doherty, representing Canada, tried to make that protest effective, it did not carry weight, and when Sir Lomer Gouin again tried to make that protest, it did not carry. I am simply taking this as an example to show that the so-called equality of representation between Great Britain and her self-governing dominions in these matters of diplomatic concern has not been satisfactory nor complete nor true to the letter or the spirit.

speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question? What good does he think that treaty would have been without article 10?

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
I am not going to enter into a discussion upon that with my hon. friend. I am simply pointing out, or giving this as an illustration, that it is not according to fact-and it could not be, as I will show in a moment-to say that the representatives of the various self-governing dominions were represented in the council of nations at Versailles on the same footing and with the same

Canada's Imperial Relations

voice as the representatives of the United Kingdom. We have an example of that later on, and again I want to show the good work and the splendid spirit evinced by Sir Robert Borden in very difficult circumstances. In the year following, when 'this treaty was brought up for ratification iby this House, he laid down this doctrine, which I may say is also mine-irrespective, of course, of the merits of the treaty:
His Majesty the King and his advisers have recognized the right o*f this parliament to express its opinion upon this treaty. I made that pledge to parliament and the British government 'have been informed of that pledge. They recognize the situation, and they are not disposed to deal with this treaty, so far as Canada is concern d, apart from the approval of the Canadian parliament.
This was challenged by Mr. Fielding, who endeavoured to make out that even if the parliament of Canada did not ratify the treaty, the treaty would go on just the same, to which argument Sir Robert Borden replied:
I am stating to the hon. gentleman an absolute fact, as to which I hope he (will not doubt my word. I toll him it is recognized by the ministers of the crown of Great Britain that this treaty must be submitted to the Canadian parliament for its approval, and that we desire, we insist, upon the judgment of the Canadian parliament in regard to it before we advise the King on behalf of Canada that the treaty should be ratified.
Again Mr. Fielding derided this pretension. He claimed this simply meant that if the treaty was not ratified the Conservative government would be defeated, to which Sir Robert Borden replied:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. He has forgotten what I said a moment ago. Failure to ratify .the treaty would involve very serious consequences indeed.
Hon. Mr. Fielding:	What are they?
Sir Robert Borden: The consequences would be that Canada would stand out of a treaty of peace accepted by the empire.
Hon. Mr. Fielding:	Would we be at war?
Sir Robert Borden:	I have already said what in
our opinion our status would be in that case. If my hon. friend means that, notwithstanding the arrangements which have been made, the conventions which have become recognized, the status which has been accorded to the Dominions during recent years, we are still subject to have this treaty ratified by His Majesty on behalf of Canada whether the parliament of Canada is willing to ratify it or not, then I tell him he is dealing in ancient history and that his ideas should advance with the progress of recent years.
Later on he adds:
His suggestion was that ratification by the parliament of Canada is merely a farce, that the government of the United Kingdom possesses such constitutional right in respect of this Dominion that they can impose their will upon us .without regard to this parliament. I repeat that if such is the opinion of the hon. member, he is thinking in terms of a hundred years ago, and not of to-day.
There Sir Robert Borden laid down quite clearly and unmistakably the doctrine that

neither the government of Canada nor the government of Great Britain can compromise the future or the present rights of the people of Canada without the explicit and expressed consent of the parliament of Canada. This is good nationalist doctrine, and I accept it when it comes from a Conservative leader just as readily as I would accept it from any other authority.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: It is good Conservative doctrine, and if I understand the statement of policy made in times past by the right hon. leader of the present government, it seems to me it is a statement of good Liberal policy as well.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
Of course; that is what I am going to prove in a moment. The only thing is I would like to have it asserted by parliament as early as possible in time of peace, when people possess their cool senses, instead of waiting for the excitement caused by the approach or the declaration of war to have it disregarded by both parties. The observation of my excellent friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) dispenses with the necessity of my .giving another quotation from Sir Robert Borden on the rights of the parliament of Canada from that same lecture at Williamstown last summer, but I may well give this short quotation, which I think was meant as a warning to London:
It will be wise for British statesmen constantly to remember that the commonwealth cannot go to war in sections, and that engagements which may involve the Dominions in war ought not to be undertaken without their full concurrence.
Now let us see how this worked out in practice after the war. Not long after the conference in 1922, came what has been called the Chanak incident. After some squabble had been going on between the Greeks and the Turks, the Turks being encouraged by the French, and the Greeks being encouraged by the British-that is a matter of history now- the matter became rather ugly. The Greeks were thrown out of Asia Minor, and of a sudden came a message from Mr. Winston Churchill to the Canadian government, as well as to the governments of the other Dominions, asking practically for a declaration of empire solidarity in the action which the British government contemplated taking in the Mediterranean. Of course, it has been explained since that this action was not very well thought out, that the British cabinet had not been consulted, and that there was not much danger; but, Sir, past experience should prove to us that even when the whole British cabinet is not consulted, that does not mean

Canada's Imperial Relations
that nothing will come out of it. At the beginning of this session I reminded the House of what is also a matter of history, that the obligations laid upon the shoulders of the people of Great Britain on behalf of France, and which eventually came with a vengeance upon our own shoulders, were undertaken solely by some members of the British government, in the ignorance of the Prime Minister of England and of two-thirds of his colleagues in the cabinet. The truth was known in the three fateful days which elapsed between the declaration of war by Germany upon France and the declaration of war by England upon Germany. So I do not think any incident of that nature can be overlooked, and I think also the present Prime Minister did the right thing by Canada, did the right thing by the British Empire, and did the right thing by the world, when he refused to be stampeded by that blackmailing process of Mr. Winston Churchill. Likewise I think he remained, absolutely faithful, in word' as in deed, to the old doctrine and the old practice of Dominion freedom of action, when he refused to be bound by the terms of the treaty of Lausanne, when he refused even to accept the invitation to be represented at Lausanne which came just a few days before the conference was opened, and when this government had not been kept in knowledge of what had elapsed since the Chanak incident, and when the conference came practically as a sequel to that incident.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman speaking with knowledge and authority on that point?

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: As to whether the government were kept informed or not during that interval?

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
I take the exchange of telegrams which has been published both in London and here, in which I find, and it has not been contradicted, that the British government assumed that the Canadian government would act at Lausanne in the same manner that it had acted at Versailles and elsewhere; to which the Canadian government replied that the case was rather different because at the Peace conference they had been invited beforehand; they had taken a share in the negotiations, and they had signed for what they were worth the treaties of peace. Of course, I cannot read the whole correspondence, but it can be found in the Sessional Papers of 1924. I will read just this one paragraph, which I think sums up the 14011-1141
whole thing. This is in the despatch of Lord Byng to the Secretary of State for the Colonies, then the Duke of Devonshire, dated December 31, 1922:
Your Gra-ce is quite right is assuming that as regards treaties in which Canada is supposed to have a direct or immediate interest, the procedure here outlined is the one which our government would wish to follow.
In the case of the main political treaties concluded since the war, .in general the rule seems to have 'been followed that, wherever the Dominions could be said to have a direct or immediate interest, the procedure was shaped to include their participation in, and signature of, the proceedings. That in the case of the conference at Lausanne a like procedure has not been followed with respect to representation and participation by Canada, has been regarded by us as evidence that in the opinion of the countries by whom the invitations to the conference at Lausanne were extended, Canada could not have been believed to have the direct and immediate interest which she was supposed to have in the conference at Versailles and Washington.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say, not that Canada had not been invited soon enough to Lausanne, but that the government of Canada had in the meantime not been kept informed as to the progress of events.

hon. member.

What I mean is that
there was not such official communication between the government in London and the various dominion governments in regard to this as there is between any full-fledged government and foreign governments with which it is allied-that is, in the way of diplomatic correspondence, such as was exchanged during the war or for some time previously, for example, between the French and English governments.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext: I read all that, but I did not place the same interpretation upon it as my hon. friend does.

subtopic: LABOUR AND THE NEW SOCIAL ORDER
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me, I will not go into the details. I am taking the official documents and trying to make out what has been the general trend of relations between the two governments. I would not like to discuss any small issue connected with any of those instances.
This was not merely a free handed or self-willed determination of this government. The attitude observed in the Chanak incident and with regard to the Lausanne treaty, one before and the other after, was in exact conformity with the principles laid down at the Imperial conference in 1923 and .adopted1 unan- ' imously by t'he conference with regard to

Canada's Imperial Relations
negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties. There for the first time-and this is one of the redeeming features in that whole history-it was fully acknowledged, unanimously acknowledged, that with regard to negotiation, signing and ratification of treaties, each portion of the British Empire stood as a unit. If the matter for negotiation concerned only one of those countries, then the treaty was to be negotiated by the representatives of that country and signed by them. If it concerned more than one, then those self-governing countries of the British Empire concerned should be represented, always with regard, of course, to the interests that might arise, or that might connect their actions with the situation of other portions of the empire. In other words, there was a return by a roundabout way to the old principle that the obligations of each portion of the British Empire are measured by their responsibilities and by their interests. Under that new rule, each country controls, or is entitled to control, its foreign affairs according to its situation and its interests, and takes part, by its representatives, in diplomatic relations or in the diplomatic conferences which deal with those things. That is practically what has been done by the present Minister of Justice in the so-called Halibut treaty. I must say that I do not attach a great deal of importance to that; but it is at least a landmark in that interesting process of evolution in our relations with the Motherland. Instead of being looked upon as a revolutionary procedure it should be accepted as a healthful sign of the development or the renascence of the sense of dignity and nationality in ithe various .portions of the empire. For my part I am prepared to congratulate this government on their attitude in those instances, just as I congratulate Sir Robert Borden in the instances I have mentioned, and just as I congratulate the right hon. leader of the opposition for his attitude in London in regard to the Japanese treaty. Why should we always look upon the action of our leading men from the small point of view which would enable one party to take advantage of the other, instead of looking to the general advantage accruing to Canada through the effort which any of its representatives may make in London or elsewhere to assert the dignity and the interests of the people of Canada?
I must say, not to be too complimentary, that I think our representation by the so-called panel system in London, the year after, is one of the most absurd things I ever heard of. The idea that the British Empire should be represented in an international congress by
[Mr. BourassaJ
the British government first, last and forever, and then in the case of the dominions, one of the dominions on Monday, another on Tuesday, another on Wednesday and the other on Thursday, is surely laughable. Of course the reason is easy to understand. Foreign nations, realizing the tremendous possibilities that might accrue from that evolution in the constitutional government of the empire, have begun to challenge the right of the dominions to be represented independently, or rather to be represented as units in an international congress. It is a well-known fact now that the dominions.could not be represented equally with the United Kingdom in London in 1925 because of the opposition of the French government, among others. Time and again I have read-not time and again, because foreigners do not take much interest in our affairs -several times I have read very thoughtful studies by foreign authorities on this situation, as it affects international affairs. They say the British Empire must make up its mind whether it is One nation or several nations. If it is one nation, then it must be represented by one authority. That authority cannot be shared, as stated by Mr. Asquith several years ago. If it is several nations, then it cannot at leisure act as one, or as six or seven, according to its fancy or its interests. I admit this is the one aspect of the question which is the most baffling at the present time. I have confidence enough in the common sense of the British people at home and abroad, and I have confidence enough, in spite of appearances, in the sense of just pride in these young nations that have grown all the world over on the pattern of the Motherland, to believe that we can solve that problem as between ourselves. But with regard to the foreign world, it must be admitted that since we have abandoned the safe and sound policy of The Fathers of Confederation, we have created a very complex- situation in our relations with the outside world. The moment we have chosen to share in the responsibilities of the empire the world over, we must be prepared to face that problem, not only from the British, not only from the Canadian, but also from the international point of view. It is worth while being considered and studied; and for that reason alone, it is urgent that the best minds of this country should give it their deepest thought as right-thinking men, in England and in the other portions of the empire, are doing now and have been doing ever since the war.
With the adjunction of the Free State of Ireland to the association of nations called the British Empire-with Lord Milner, I do

Canada's Imperial Relations
not like the term "British Empire;" I think it is a, misnomer-a new phase has developed. As the hon. member for Winnipeg Nor-th Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) pointed out this afternoon, the constitution of the Free State of Ireland is in advance of our constitution. Between the two stands the constitution of Australia, which in some respects is in advance of ours and in some respects backward of that of Ireland. Last year, in Washington, at the interparliamentary conference, Mr. Fitzgerald, foreign minister in Dublin and representative of the Free State of Ireland at that conference, suggested that the British Dominions should assert their right to remain neutral in any war in which Great Britain or other portions of the empire might be engaged, and that this should be recognized internationally. Of course, the resolution was withdrawn. Numerous articles appeared in England, but more so in Canada than in England, denouncing this as a novelty, as a suggestion of secession.
It is strange how the drifting policy which we have followed for twenty-five years should have made so many of us forget the elements of our national history. As far back as 1862 the same idea was suggested in Montreal by another Irishman, it is true, but I hope this in itself does not discredit the contention. He said:
The present is not the fittest time, nor is the hustings the fittest (place, to enter fuMy into the subject of our colonial defences. I will only say for myself, gentlemen, what you, as my electors have a right to know, that while I am thoroughly convinced the connection with the Mother Country ought to be an object, of attachment with us, second only to the love we bear to our own institutions-that while I believe next to England our duty is to cultivate a good understanding with the United States-that having these maxims to steer by, on the right hand and the left, I am still of opinion, speaking as a Canadian publicist, that some recognized international status must be found for this country which will preserve her better than any armed force, from being made the battleground of quarrels, which she can neither make or avoid.
He suggested finally-
Some such arrangement as established the neutrality of Greece in 1831, and the neutrality of Belgium in 1839. With such an arrangement our own militia would be quite adequate for an internal defence, and Great Britain would be honourably relieved from the anxiety and outlay of her Canadian garrisons.
This was suggested in 1862 by Thomas D'Aroy McGee, who a few days later became a member of the Canadian government, and who two years later entered into the coalition government which made confederation. I find no trace in the journals or the public expressions of the day that anybody was scandalized by that. Whether agreed to or not, everybody seemed to think that it was a fair point for discussion. So much was this the
case that at the opening of the next session that speech was reproduced and added to the debates of the House as a very valuable contribution to the great subject of the relations between Great Britain and Canada. More than that, when three years later Sir John A. Macdonald presented the Quebec resolution before the parliament assembled here, on what basis did he ask for the approval of the parliament and the people of Canada? That under those new terms of nationhood Canada was looking for a "permanent alliance'' with Great Britain which she hoped would be reciprocated; but in the very same sentence he reserved to Canada the right to form alliances with foreign nations. Just imagine, Sir, the idea that Canada could, of her own free will, make alliances with foreign nations without regard to whether that pleased the people in London or not! That was not the saying of a striker in Winnipeg or of a French rebel in the province of Quebec who will not stand up every time or place the national anthem is sung. No, it was stated by the leader of the LiberalAHonservative party, by the chief of the coalition government which made confederation, and it was stated as the principle upon which Canada would stand henceforth in her relations with Great Britain.
Why, then, should it be improper to think and to state that in readjusting our terms of partnership with Great Britain we should come back to t'he sound policy that was laid down in those days by the men who succeeded in reconciling race with race, in adjusting provincial differences, in doing away with all the bitter remembrances of the past; who destroyed, both in England and in Canada, the idea that secession was unavoidable, because it was impossible to get along? It was by relying upon the sense of nationhood of the Canadian people and upon the common sense and sense of fair play of the British people that confederation was made possible. I admit it is perfectly legitimate to look to something else, to look to closer partnership, to unity of action in time of peace and war. I have no grudge against those who hold that doctrine as the proper one, but I would1 simply ask them and the people of Canada to think a little over the consequences.
England is a world power; she rules the vastest and most complex empire that has ever existed, not only because it covers more land and contains more inhabitants than any other human conglomeration of the past, but because it is scattered on all continents of the earth and therefore raises problems of a complexity and diversity such as no other nation has ever been called upon to consider and to solve. Surely it is a great testimony to the
Canada's Imperial Relations

political1 genius of the British nation, to the marvellous tradition of policy of her ruling men, whether kings, statesmen or leaders of opinion, that England could have got along, especially during the last century and a half, carrying that extraordinary burden. Let us leave aside the stock phrases about philanthropy and duty to humanity. No, the English conquered their empire for their interest first. But they rule it with genius, and administer it with perhaps a lesser proportion of injustice than any other nation. And that is saying much. So far as we are concerned, however, let us consider for a moment what it means
Take the situation of England in Europe. A century ago, England was allied, with Austria and Russia to fight France; and after France had been defeated, England had a rapprochement with her, and later fought with her for Turkey against Russia, and in contradiction of Austria's interests in the near Orient. A few years later one of the wisest statesmen of England, Lord Salisbury, said that the English had ridden the wrong horse. We were not concerned with that. But if the present doctrine had prevailed then, I suppose we should have been called upon to fight against France at a certain period and with France at some other time. Then came the reaction of the sixties, when England, without actually fighting, upheld morally and diplomatically the policy of Prussia and of united Italy against France and assisted coolly in the defeat of France in 1870. It was in those days that such a wise and thorough English statesman as Lord Stanley expressed this view in the House of Lords:
The government and the people of this country have seen with entire acquiescence, and even, I believe, with approval, the enormous aggrandisement which has accrued to Germany, or rather to Prussia.
That was three years before the Franco-Prussian war, one year after Sadowa, and three years after Prussia had deprived little Denmark of the whole of Holstein and a part of Schleswig. I am not saying that the British were wrong. I am merely pointing out how complex a situation exists in Europe, and showing that British statesmen must change their policy according to the circumstances, the needs and the interests which they are obliged to meet. But it does not follow that we should acquiesce, especially to the point of being prepared to shed blood and contribute money eveiy time they choose to alter their policy.
About ten years later, Great Britain stands alongside Germany and France, against Russia, in negotiating the Berlin treaty, in preparing the way to the Balkan crisis which precipitated the last war. Then she favours the Triple

Alliance against France and Russia; then she allies herself with Japan to crush Russia in Manchuria in 1905, and looks complacently upon the development of the Central Europe policy of Germany and Austria, to the extent that the Bagdad railway was first brought to the attention of Europe and of European finance by the London press. So sympathetic was England at that time to German policy as against the Russian and the French. It was in those years that Mr. Chamberlain launched his famous appeal, to the United States on the one side, and to Germany on the other, to consummate the consolidation of the Teutonic races to counteract the influence of the Latins and the Slavs. But there was a sudden reversal of policy. The moment Germany began to develop her naval programme, the moment her fleet became a menace to the sea power of England, British statesmen saw the necessity for changing their policy. I do not blame them for that But what was the result? The result was that in less than five years the astounded world saw England, France, Russia and Japan allied against Germany, Austria and Turkey. The war being over, we again see England preparing for a reversal of policy to side with Germany and Italy against France and the Balkan countries. Again, I say, I do not blame her. On the contrary, I think her statesmen are very wise and far-seeing.
At the beginning of the war when our newspapers were filled with denunciations of the wild Huns, with the darkest pictures of the horrors that would befall Canada, should Germany win the war, I had the advantage of meeting an accredited English publicist, with the best letters of introduction that could be had from the British authorities. I asked him what he expected would be the result not, of course, of the war-he did not know any more about that than I did-but of British policy after the war. I wanted to find out from him what he thought would be the next turn in that policy. "How is it", I asked him, "that the sentiment in Great Britain against Germany has grown so suddenly?" He answered: "For the simple reason that we discovered that they were getting better than ourselves at our own game." I asked him what he meant. "I mean," he said, "at the game of settling colonies and building navies. They are improving upon us in this game and we will not let them get the better of us." I asked him further what England would do in relation to Asia Minor after Germany had been crushed. I did not know then of the secret treaties under which Sir Eward Grey, our spokesman, the spokesman of the empire, had

Canada's Imperial Relations
given a free hand to Russia over Turkey, including Constantinople, and had agreed with the French government in one month to hand over a certain piece of territory to Greece and the next month to Italy, the difference being that in one treaty the same territory was called North Epirus, to satisfy Greece, while in the other it was described as South Albania, to please Italy. I asked this gentleman what he thought England's policy would be after the war. In reply he declared that the moment the end seemed imminent, just before Germany was crushed, England would form an alliance with Germany to keep Russia down. I said, "Do you think you will bring the French to agree to that?" He replied, "They will have to agree, for if they don't we will isolate them." That was practically five years in anticipation of the policy which began to assert itself in Genoa, which asserted itself still more clearly in London and also at Lausanne, and which was apparent, with a slight modification, at Geneva this year. But wait until next year.
Once more, I repeat, I do not blame England. For their own good and for the good of Europe, British statesmen have changed their policy after each war. As Mr. Lloyd George said on one occasion, "My attitude at Genoa was exactly the attitude of Lord Castlereagh at Vienna. Just as Lord Castle-reagh prevented Austria and Prussia from crushing France, because England's interest did not lie in the direction of crushing a great nation, so I do not want France to crush Germany." That, I say, is good policy, inasmuch as it makes for the peace of Europe and of the world. For that reason I have, time and again, to the great scandal of some of my friends in the province of Quebec, praised the policy pursued by England after the war, because it conduced to peace. But after this war is forgotten, we should be careful of England's policy, because then, it will likely lead us into another war; and that, not because England wants war, but because, in view of her enormous possessions, it is imperative that she shall remain mistress of the seas. England so long as she remains mistress of the seas over which is flung the greatest empire that has ever existed, is 'bound to go to war to crush any nation that threatens her naval supremacy or her colonial power.
Well, we are a young nation with a population little larger than that of the city of London, scattered over a territory as vast as Europe. Is it, then, socially right; is it politically right; is it British-like, that we should impose upon the future generations of this country burdens of empire equal to those which the people of England must bear of
necessity because of England's unique situation and because of the tremendous responsibilities which she must inevitably shoulder?
So far I have been speaking only of the situation of England in Europe. Just this week I was reading a protest from the mouthpiece of the ultra-loyalist element of Cape Colony, the Cape Times, reminding the British government about Locarno:
Great Britain is bo occupied with the confused currents of European diplomacy that she has forgotten that she represents the British Empire. The British partnership is the greatest power in the world as long as it speaks with one voice, and Great Britain should speak not as a European power, but as a delegate of the empire, and refuse to be drawn into the vortex of European complications.
It is easy to say that in Cape Town, but not so easy to put it into action in London, on the borders of Europe. But this precisely opens the door to the other aspect of the situation. After all, England is a secondary power in Europe. She is a first-class power only on account of her navy. And she has her navy on account of her possessions-not for our protection, but for the protection of her water routes, to keep the avenues of trade open so as to give nourishment to her people and to bring raw materials to her industries. The day that England loses her empire and her navy, that day she would come down to about the level of Holland after that country lost its navy and practically had to rely on the grace of England and the other great maritime nations for the retention of her colonies. But nevertheless it is true that England is much more of an Asiatic power than a European, nearly as much of an American power, and of course much more of an African power than either an Asiatic or American. Well, what does that mean? It means that England in her relations with the rest of the world, with Europe as well as with her dominions, is obliged to think all the time of India, of Egypt, of Asia Minor, of Africa-painted in red from Cape Town to Cairo-of Australia, of Canada. She cannot disconnect any portion of her policy from her general situation in the world. This is an evidence of her tremendous imperial genius, but it makes a problem that is rather hard to deal with for a small growing nation such as we are with the tremendous home responsibilities that we have. Take her Asiatic and African policy; for a century at least it has been dominated by the simple fact of her possession of India. Let us look at one single aspect of that relationship-Hindu emigration to the other portions of the empire. Our friends from British Columbia, would not, I think, be prepared to agree that in order to make the government of England easier in India they should open

Canada's Imperial Relations
the doors of their province to Hindu immigration; but if they looked at the question from the imperial point of view they would see the other aspect. I remember being in London just at the time when our naval policies were so tremendously discussed here. I was asking a high official of the India office in London: What is really the best contribution that Canada could render to the imperial cause? "If you could bring British Columbia to open her doors to Hindu immigration, that would be worth all the dreadnaughts you could build in ten years." Well, that is an aspect of the imperial question. The Australians see it from another point of view. But that is not all. There is Persia, as my hon. friend stated this afternoon, there is Irak, there is Palestine, there is Egypt, there is Morocco.
But let us come to America and terminate there our review of British policy and Imperial entanglements in the last century. Strange to say-and I do not think I am boasting in saying it-I stand as perhaps the only Canadian public man who on the whole has upheld British policy as applied to American affairs. I well remember at the time of the Alaska boundary award, when I was denounced in this House of Commons as a traitor to my country because I stated that Lord Alverstone's decision was sound according to law and to fact. I still believe it. I know that numerous writings have appeared, mostly in Toronto, denouncing British diplomacy as regards Canada. I do not view it that way. Of course, we boast very much about the century of peace between this country and the United States. Undoubtedly we owe it to a large extent to the common sense of the Canadian people; but we owe it also to the common sense of the British people; and when we were accusing Great Britain of sacrificing our interests for ithe sake of maintaining peace with the United States,
I think we were making a mistake. England was doing the only thing she could do in that respect. I never understood it better than on my second last- visit in London, a few months before the war. At that time there was a great deal of discussion about difficulties in Europe, Irish affairs, and all that. We had had our two squabbles about naval policy-naval contribution as proposed by the Conservative party and a so-called Canadian navy .as proposed by the Liberal party. I had an excellent occasion to get opinions on the merits of those policies from two of the most respected British authorities on naval matters-authorities whose opinions I valued much because they were generally in absolute contradiction to each other; I mean

the late Lord Charles Beresford and the late Lord Fisher. Norv the two old sea-dogs have gone to their reward, I hope that on the other side of the world they are not quarreling as much as they did while here, and I think I can without any indiscretion repeat exactly what they told me.
Of course, Lord Charles Beresford's opinion w7as well known. On the one hand, he did not believe in the dreadnaught policy. Then he had expressed himself quite openly on the Monroe doctrine as being the main safeguard of British possessions in America. But with regard to Lord Fisher, I did not know. So I went to him and asked what he thought of our two naval policies. " Well," he said, " my good fellow, I don't think much of either. Of course, if you have money to squander you may do anything you like, but if you regard it either from the naval point of view or from the national point of view for your protection, it is a great mistake. Don't make any mistake, England will never spend one penny and will never shoot one gun to defend Canada against the United States-simply because we cannot do it. It is just as well you should understand it. It would not be rendering service to you to fight the United States, either for Canada or for anything else. If you need help as against any other country, you must not count on us; you must count on the United States. If you want to make an arrangement for national defence, don't come to London; go to Washington." " Well," I said, " that would be very ill received by our super-patriots and imperialists in Canada." " Ah," he said, " are you so foolish as that in Canada? Don't you realize that the whole world's policy is based on inter-dependence?
I think we British have some degree of national pride, and yet we rely upon the French army to fight for us against Germany, just as France relies upon our navy to fight against the German navy, just as in times past Germany relied upon us to give her money to fight against France. The whole of the world's relations is based on interdependence. How can you imagine that you, a small nation of nine million people scattered over a country as large as the continent of Europe, alongside a nation of a hundred and ten million people, can count upon the support of a fleet in Europe,-the main use of which is to keep our sea routes open-to defend your own land against the richest and most powerful country on earth? Of course,
I repeat that if you have money to squander, throw it in the water if you like; it does well there from a sentimental point of view. We cannot stop you, but really we do not need your money; you had better keep it at home."

So I came back convinced that in opposing any such policy, while I might be styled a traitor in Canada, there might still be a few men in England, whose names are connected with England's power and glory, who have enough British common sense to understand that Canada should look on her own situation as Great Britain looks on hers.
I thought that was sound advice then, Sir, and I think it is sound advice now. Why do we not come to a reality? Why do we not come back to the old principle which was so strongly enunciated by Sir John A. Macdonald, and later by Sir Charles Tupper? There is no man I know of in our Canadian history who resented so strongly as Sir Charles Tupper the accusation that Canada was a sponger upon the British nation because she did not contribute to the maintenance of the British navy and army. I know of no Canadian and no Britisher who ever brought out so strongly, and with such explicit facts, the evidence that by building up our territory, by bringing in population, by being peaceful here and making Canada strong we were making our best contribution to the British Empire. That was the way I looked at things twenty-five years ago and I confess that it is still my view. It seems to me there is no harm in asking the Canadian people to look over these things, to compare the policies pursued in late years and what they have cost Canada, with no real profit to Canada and the empire, with the results obtained by the humbler but more practical policy enacted by constructive statesmen of sixty years ago, who based all our relations with Great Britain upon the sound principle that each country should look to itself and leave the British statesmen to look after the general affairs of the empire.
These ideas are growing; they are having a rebirth, so to speak, in the minds of many people. A year or so ago, I think, Sir Clifford Sifton, once a member of the Liberal party and another time an ally of the Conservative party, whose policy may be open to discussion on many issues, but whose common sense and keen mind no one will dispute, put that problem before the people of Toronto in as clear and unequivocal a manner as it could be put. It is not so long ago that an English imperialist, one who knows much about Canada, Mr. Percy Hurd, in the House of Commons in England, reminded the English rulers that they should not forget that Canada has interests in America which are not the interests of Europe, and that Australia has interests in the Pacific ocean which are not the interests of Canada.
Now, Sir, our connection with the British Empire may last long or may terminate abruptly. For my part I stated twenty-five years ago, at the time of the South African war, and I state again to-night with the same conviction, that I am not longing for secession.
I believe we need for a long time, not the protection of Great Britain; I do not think Great Britain can afford us any protection that we are in need of, but I prize the association with Great Britain. I repeat, without any idea of offending members of this House or anyone of English stock; that I appreciate that link with Great Britain in a certain degree more than they can, because it is an appreciation based on study and on reflection; it is not the voice of blood. You cannot expect the French-Canadians to love the British; why should they? But you may expect the French-Canadians at ail times to appreciate their connection with Great Britain. For my part I appreciate it more, perhaps, than a great many other French-Canadians, because I have frequently been in Great Britain and have, so to speak, imbibed the atmosphere of British political life. And why have I been so often in trouble in this country? It is because I have persisted in thinking that I could have the same freedom of thought and language in this country as is enjoyed in England, and I propose to stand by that contention. I believe the association with Great Britain is needed by us for a long time, in order to help in developing our minds to the same broad standard of individual and political liberty. I believe the association with Great Britain is a great help to us if we view it in the right way, and if we act upon it with the same British spirit of self-determination and selfrespect. But I repeat, Sir, that it is not by playing the servile worshipper of everything English that we are going to benefit by that association.. On the contrary it is by standing up in the face of Great Britain, not in a defiant attitude but in an attitude of selfrespect and virile admiration, asserting to Great Britain that there are certain matters upon which we can agree with her, and that there are other matters upon which we cannot agree, because they have interests which are not the same as ours and because we have trusts to perform and to hand over to generations to come with which neither the Englishman nor the Australian can deal for us. We have a duty to perform by Canada; the Australian has a duty to perform by Australia, and the British have a duty to Great Britain which no other country can accomplish. If we only revive these principles, these elementary truths in the minds of the people of this country or in the other portions of the

empire, I am quite sure that this great problem of inter-imperial relations will soon be solved.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to vote for the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). I think, with all due respect to him, that it is rather narrow in its wording. On the other hand I will not associate myself with those who denounce him for bringing forward the motion. Whatever 11 p.m. be the wording, I consider that the hon. gentleman has rendered service to this country and has done his duty in proposing this motion. But I would respectfully suggest an amendment to the motion, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), which is as follows:
That this be referred to the select standing committee on Industrial and International Relations for consideration and study, with power to invite expert advice, such committee to report to the House during the present session.
I suggest, for example, that that committee invite such men as Mr. Ewart, Sir John Willison, Sir Robert Falconer, Mr. Skelton, Under Secretary of State; men holding various opinions on this problem, who would come and give us their view of what some would call the imperial solution and others the national solution, and even the solution of independence. Why should we be less free in our minds than the men of sixty years ago? Are some hon. members of this House so afraid of their loyalty that they cannot hear anyone proclaim Canada's right to independence, as our forefathers did? In order to show my spirit in proposing this amendment, I would suggest-not as a motion but as a mere suggestion to the committee- that, in the opinion of this House, Canada is not bound by any obligation assumed by the government of the United Kingdom, in matters of foreign policy, unless and until the government of Canada, duly authorized by parliament, expresses its adherence thereto.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I shall not speak very long, but I would like to say a few words on this resolution.
In the first place, I take exception to the form of the resolution. I think I might make the same comment on it that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Kennedy) did. I do not see how we can be called on to pass a resolution refusing to accept a responsibility when we have never been asked to accept it. I have another objection to the resolution, and that is that it raises indirectly the question of the future status of this Dominion, whether we are to stay out of the empire or not. I think a question of that importance should not be raised in this indirect way. It seems to me that if a matter of that kind is to be discussed it should be brought up by the government and some statement of government policy be given on the subject, in order that we may have a proper debate carried on from day to day, and that everybody may have a chance to express his opinion.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has spoken to us a long time this evening on a great many subjects. May I suggest to him that when he is discussing a matter of this kind-really an important problem-he ought not to go over the whole past history of this

Canada's Imperial Relations
Dominion? As a matter of fact one is not surprised that he should remember with pride some of the things in the history of his ancestors, but the fact remains that we are now in the year 1926, and, as he said at the end of his speech, many things happened during the war. Precedents were created. Sir Robert Borden took a stand for this country which has never been equalled by any other Canadian statesman, a stand which resulted in our being recognized in every way as a nation having complete authority in all matters, not only of domestic concern, but in regard to outside questions affecting us as well.
Remarks have been made again this evening about our autonomy. Somebody said that it was absolutely unfettered and complete, a quotation, if I remember rightly from Mr. Asquith. The time has long since passed, Mr. Speaker, when any effort is being made in the Old Country to bring pressure on us, and no such effort will be made. No statesman over there would for a moment suggest that any pressure should be brought to bear on this country, and there is not a man in Canada, so far as I know, who would give up in the slightest degree our powers and our rights of self-government. Those things are all settled; we have got them; we are going to keep them; they are acknowledged by everyone; so why raise the question here? Why take up the time of this House in killing a dead horse?-for that is really what a great deal of this discussion amounts to.
The question before this country to-day and the empire is this: Can we so arrange matters that six independent countries shall work together in matters of foreign affairs and common concern? I am going to criticize this government for not taking some steps that I think they might have taken to help us along with this problem; and that could be accomplished by continuous consultation with the Motherland and with the other parts of the empire.
As I understand it, the great bulk of the people of this country want to continue our connection with the British Empire. The hon. member for Labelle this evening left me in a bit of a doubt. When he commenced his speech he said that he desired that the connection with Great Britain should be preserved, but when he came toward the end of his speech I could not make out where he stood, and I do not know now whether he thinks we should be independent or should continue as part of the British commonwealth of nations. However, the Prime Minister of this country, speaking in this House on June 9, 1924, stated his position. After oeinting
out that there were three avenues of political development, he said:
For my own part, I believe that the future of thi* Dominion will be happiest and best, most prosperous, and in every way most to the good, if its development is along the line on which it has been thus far, towards a fuller recognition of national status within that community of free nations which comprise the British Empire.
He went on to say that the imperial parliament was not a possible thing, and an imperial council was a thoroughly bad thing.
I entirely agree with him in both these statements, and in the idea that our best chance for future development lies within the British commonwealth of nations. But what has the Prime Minister done, and what has the government done, to try to bring that about? What have they done to further our relations with the rest of the empire?
In connection with our desiring to remain a part of the British Empire, I want to read from a statement which quotes a remark made by General Smuts, a man of as great ability,
I think, as anybody I have ever known. It quotes General Smuts as follows:
The empire was a priceless blessing and was to-day, with American abstention from the league, the main force supporting the advance of great human causes and ideals in the world. The maintenance of solidarity and a united front were therefore essential.
If we are to maintain the British commonwealth of nations we shall have to have more consultations from day to day than we have at the present time. We have to find some way, in between the Imperial conferences, by which we can have this consultation which is absolutely essential to our getting on together and seeing eye to eye in regard to matters of foreign affairs and common concern. As to the necessity of that and as to the feeling that people in England have on the subject, I want to read a couple of extracts. In the first place, Mr. Austen Chamberlain, when he brought in the Locarno treaty, referring to the Dominions, said:
Their liberty and freedom of action are safeguarded specifically under the treaty. It is recognized that only their own governments, acting with the authority of their own parliament, can undertake for them the obligations that we are asking the House of Commons to undertake for Great Britain, but we hope that we may discuss this matter fully whenever the next Imperial conference is set up, and that that Imperial conference 'may not be too long delayed. I do not think that it is possible to treat matters of this great consequence, covering so wide a field, by dispatch or cable across thousands of miles of ocean. For a true appreciation of the .position personal contact and personal explanation are necessary.
Now Mr. Chamberlain states a truth which we all know, namely, that you cannot discuss intricate and delicate matters unless you are
